questions.stem: Your programme charter for a water utility carries one objective: make the supply network more resilient. Reviewing the three workstream plans before baselining, you find the treatment lead has planned against contamination, the network lead against burst mains in cold weather, and the digital lead against loss of the control room. Each plan is competent, and each quotes the same charter sentence back to you. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Baseline all three plans, since each reading is legitimate and together they cover more failure modes.
options.rationale: This mistakes coverage for agreement. Three readings feel like breadth until the budget is cut, at which point nobody can say which resilience the programme was funded to buy and the cut is made by whoever argues hardest.

options.text: Take the three readings to the sponsor and steering group, ask which failures the programme exists to prevent, and rewrite the objective in those terms.
options.rationale: The divergence is evidence that the objective was never agreed, only approved. Putting the three readings in front of the people who own the objective forces the choice that the original wording let everyone avoid.

options.text: Select the reading with the strongest business case and instruct the other two leads to replan against it.
options.rationale: It substitutes the project manager's judgement for the sponsor's on a question of what the organisation wants. It also throws away the useful signal that three competent people read one sentence three ways.

options.text: Add an agreed definition of resilience to the programme glossary and circulate it to all three workstreams.
options.rationale: This treats a governance disagreement as a vocabulary problem. A definition nobody negotiated changes no plan, because each lead already believes their reading is the definition.

questions.explanation: An objective phrased at the level of a virtue will be agreed by everyone and will constrain no one. The working test of a statement of purpose is whether it can refuse something: if no plausible plan is ruled out by it, it is a slogan rather than an objective, and the disagreement it hides surfaces later as a fight over scope or money. Divergent plans built on identical wording are the earliest cheap warning that this has happened.
questions.mindset: An objective that cannot rule anything out has not been agreed, however fluently it is quoted.

questions.stem: A developer joining your product team asks, in her first week, what the product is actually for. The only artefact you can point her to is the slide the sponsor used at the funding board, which names three target markets and a revenue figure. The team has been delivering for four months and nobody has asked the question before. What is the best first response?

options.text: Send her the sponsor's funding slide and suggest she will pick the rest up from the team over her first few sprints.
options.rationale: A funding artefact says why the organisation invested, not what the team is for, and absorption by osmosis is what produced four months of nobody being able to answer. It also makes the newest person responsible for assembling something the team should hold.

options.text: Give her your own understanding now, then put the question to the whole team so they produce a statement they can all give.
options.rationale: The question is answered immediately for her and treated as evidence for everyone else. That a new joiner had to ask is the finding, and it belongs to the team rather than to her induction.

options.text: Tell her the product backlog is the most accurate guide to what the product is for.
options.rationale: The backlog records what is being built next, which is a decision downstream of purpose rather than a statement of it. Reading intent backwards out of a work queue is exactly how a team ends up serving the queue.

options.text: Explain that the vision is the product owner's responsibility and point her to them.
options.rationale: It routes a reasonable question into a role boundary. Ownership of the artefact may sit with the product owner, but a purpose only one person can state is not shared, which is the whole point of having one.

questions.explanation: The first person to ask what the work is for is rarely the only person who does not know; they are the only one who has not yet learned that asking is unusual. Treat the question as a measurement of the team rather than a gap in one person's induction, and answer it in a form the team can repeat without you. Purpose that lives in one head is a single point of failure with a friendly face.
questions.mindset: Treat a newcomer's naive question as a reading of the team, not a gap in the newcomer.

questions.stem: You ran a half-day session with a hybrid programme's twenty-strong core team and its four business leads, and it produced a one-page statement of what the programme is for that everyone in the room endorsed. Two weeks later you notice the statement has not been referred to in any planning session, stand-up or steering paper since, and no decision has been argued in its terms. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Require every prioritisation decision to record which part of the statement it serves, in the meeting where prioritisation already happens.
options.rationale: A statement becomes real at the moment it changes an outcome. Attaching it to a decision point that already exists makes it load-bearing rather than decorative, and costs no new ceremony.

options.text: Ask the four business leads to use the statement in their own forums, in their own words, rather than relying on you to repeat it.
options.rationale: Purpose that only the project manager voices is heard as project communications. Coming from the leads their people already answer to, it is heard as what the organisation now wants.

options.text: Re-run the workshop with the wider programme so more people have been through the same exercise.
options.rationale: It answers a problem of use with more production. The room agreed the statement without difficulty; repeating the agreement does not address that nothing downstream has changed.

options.text: Publish the statement on the programme wiki, the team room wall and the footer of the status report.
options.rationale: Visibility is the cheapest available action and the one most often mistaken for adoption. People already endorsed the words; putting them where they can be seen does not make anyone reason with them.

options.text: Survey the team in a month to test how many can recall the statement accurately.
options.rationale: It measures recall, which was never the failure. A team can quote a sentence perfectly and still decide as though it did not exist, so the survey would report success on the wrong variable.

questions.explanation: Agreement in a workshop is cheap because nothing has yet been given up for it. A statement of purpose earns its place only when it is wired into a decision that recurs and is repeated by the people whose authority the audience already recognises. Reinforcement through publication and recall tests measures whether the words travelled, when the question is whether the reasoning did.
questions.mindset: Judge a statement of purpose by the decisions it has changed, not by how many people can recite it.

questions.stem: A baggage system replacement at a regional airport does its cutover work overnight. The day-shift handlers attended the briefing on why the system is being replaced, fewer misdirected bags for connecting passengers, and repeat it readily. The night shift, who do most of the physical installation, have received the schedule and the method statements and nothing else. Their supervisor mentions that his crew assume the whole thing is a cost exercise aimed at them. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Run the same briefing at a time the night shift actually works, delivered with someone they already know and trust.
options.rationale: The gap is one of reach, not content, and it was created by scheduling the briefing around the project's convenience. Delivering it in their hours through a familiar voice removes both the practical and the credibility barrier.

options.text: Ask the supervisor to pass on the reasoning at the next shift handover.
options.rationale: It delegates the message to someone who has not been briefed to give it and who currently believes the assumption himself. Second-hand transmission of intent is where nuance and conviction are lost.

options.text: Add a paragraph explaining the rationale to the front of the method statements.
options.rationale: It puts purpose inside a document read for instructions under time pressure at three in the morning. Attaching intent to a procedural artefact is a way of recording that you told them, not of their hearing it.

options.text: Accept the situation, since the installation work is fully specified and does not depend on the crew knowing the rationale.
options.rationale: It assumes specified work needs no judgement, when the night shift will meet every unforeseen condition first and decide alone how to handle it. A crew that thinks the project is aimed at them also reports problems more slowly.

questions.explanation: Whether a purpose has been communicated is a question about who was in the room, not about what was said, and the people most often missed are those whose hours or location differ from the project's own. The groups furthest from the briefing are frequently the ones making the most unsupervised decisions. Assume that any explanation delivered once, in core hours, has reached only the population that keeps those hours.
questions.mindset: Ask who was not in the room before concluding that a message has landed.

questions.stem: Your team is building traceability software for a dairy co-operative because new regulation requires it. In the retrospective the team call the work box-ticking and describe the real product work as on hold until it is done. Velocity is steady, but two developers have started skipping refinement. You know the regulation exists because a contaminated batch took nine days to trace and reached three counties before it was found. What should you do?

options.text: Bring the team into contact with the people who ran that nine-day trace, so they hear what the delay cost and what would have shortened it.
options.rationale: The disengagement comes from the work having a legal reason and no human one. Contact with the people who lived the failure supplies a purpose the team can own, which no restatement of the regulation can.

options.text: Acknowledge that the work is unrewarding and commit to a date after which the team returns to product features.
options.rationale: It confirms the team's framing that this is not real work, and buys short-term goodwill by conceding the point. The quality risk lasts as long as the belief does, and the belief has just been endorsed.

options.text: Raise the skipped refinement with the two developers' line managers as a performance matter.
options.rationale: It treats a symptom of lost meaning as a discipline problem, which usually restores compliance and deepens the disengagement. The other developers will read it as confirmation that the work cannot be defended on its merits.

options.text: Add the specific regulatory clause to each story so the team can see exactly what compels the work.
options.rationale: Citing the clause answers the question the team is not asking. They already know they are compelled; what is missing is why the requirement is worth meeting well rather than minimally.

questions.explanation: Mandated work arrives with a reason attached that explains the obligation but not its value, and a team that can only see the obligation will meet it at the lowest passing standard. Purpose has to be traced past the rule to the harm the rule exists to prevent, and it lands hardest when it comes from the people who experienced that harm rather than from the project manager. Compliance framing produces compliance-grade work.
questions.mindset: Behind every mandate there is a harm someone actually suffered; that, not the mandate, is the purpose.

questions.stem: You have been asked to advise on three programmes in the same portfolio, each of which has been described to you as having a communication problem. Reading the evidence, you conclude that shared purpose has failed in a different way in each case, and that more communication would help none of them. Match each symptom to the intervention that addresses its cause. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Every workstream lead quotes the same objective accurately, and their plans optimise for visibly different things.
The team can state the purpose correctly and cannot name a single request it would rule out.
A supplier delivers exactly what the specification requires and misses what the work was for.

options.text: Have the sponsor rank the competing readings and restate the objective as the one the programme is funded for.
options.rationale: Divergent plans under identical wording mean the objective is ambiguous rather than unclear, and ambiguity is resolved by whoever owns the money choosing between the readings. Nothing the workstreams do among themselves can settle it.

options.text: Walk through recent real decisions and record which way the purpose would have sent each one.
options.rationale: A purpose with no refusals in it has never been tested against anything concrete. Replaying decisions that have already happened makes the boundary visible without anyone having to defend a live request.

options.text: Put the intent alongside the requirement in the statement of work, and review deliverables against both.
options.rationale: A supplier held only to the specification will optimise for the specification, correctly. Making intent contractually visible is what lets a compliant but useless deliverable be discussed before it is accepted.

options.text: Increase the frequency of programme communications so the purpose is repeated more often.
options.rationale: Not used. Repetition is the standard reflex and none of these three is a shortage of exposure: in each case the purpose has been heard accurately and has failed to govern anything. Saying it again more often changes none of the three causes.

questions.explanation: Failures of shared purpose look alike from a distance and have different causes, so the intervention has to follow the diagnosis. Ambiguity needs someone with authority to choose; an untested statement needs contact with real decisions; a contracted party needs intent written where it is enforceable. Reaching for more communication is the response that fits none of them, and it is the most common one because it is the cheapest to start.
questions.mindset: Diagnose which part of shared purpose has failed before reaching for the communication that fixes only one of them.

questions.stem: A retail bank's product team works under a vision statement agreed by the executive: to delight every customer, every time. Asked whether to build a faster card-freeze flow or a clearer overdraft warning first, three team members cite the vision and arrive at opposite answers. The product owner tells you the statement came from the executive committee and is not open to change. What should you do?

options.text: Agree a narrower product-level statement beneath the executive one, naming who this team serves and what it will not do.
options.rationale: It supplies the specificity the decision needs without picking a fight over an artefact that is doing a different job at a different level. A corporate statement can contain a sharper one; it cannot substitute for it.

options.text: Escalate to have the executive statement rewritten so it can settle questions like this one.
options.rationale: It spends credibility on changing an artefact that is not really wrong for its purpose, and a statement broad enough to cover a whole bank cannot also arbitrate one team's sprint. The escalation would likely fail and would mark the team as difficult.

options.text: Settle it on value estimates alone, since both items plainly serve customers.
options.rationale: Value cannot be estimated without saying value to whom and for what, so this defers the purpose question rather than avoiding it. It also quietly hands the decision to whoever builds the estimate.

options.text: Run a customer survey and build whichever option customers rate more highly.
options.rationale: It converts a judgement about what the team is for into a popularity measure, and both options would poll well. Preference data cannot tell you which of two goods this team exists to deliver.

questions.explanation: Statements of purpose operate at levels, and a statement written to unify an organisation is usually too broad to decide anything for one team. The remedy is a narrower statement nested beneath it rather than a campaign against it, and the test of the narrower one is that it names an exclusion. A purpose that endorses every option is indistinguishable from having none.
questions.mindset: Nest a sharper purpose beneath a broad one rather than arguing with the broad one.

questions.stem: You are automating a manual document-indexing bureau. The eleven bureau staff are your only source of the rules the system must encode, and they understand that success means their unit closes. Two have begun giving answers you can tell are incomplete; a third has become unusually thorough. Human resources has confirmed internally that redeployment will be offered but has announced nothing, and your elicitation workshops run for another five weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Press the sponsor and human resources to make the redeployment position concrete and announce it now.
options.rationale: You are asking eleven people to hand over the knowledge that currently makes them necessary while their own future is undecided. Until that is settled, incomplete answers are a rational response and no amount of facilitation will fix them.

options.text: Reconstruct the indexing rules from a large sample of historical documents instead of relying on the staff.
options.rationale: It recasts a problem of trust as a problem of data. Samples reveal the common cases, while the value of eleven experienced people is the exceptions, which are precisely what will not appear often enough to be inferred.

options.text: Tell the team that full cooperation will be reflected in how redeployment decisions are made.
options.rationale: It makes candour a condition of employment and turns the elicitation into a negotiation under duress. People will supply volume rather than accuracy, and you will not be able to tell the difference.

options.text: Concentrate the remaining workshops on the thorough third member, who is clearly willing to help.
options.rationale: It rewards the cooperative person with all the work and treats one person's account as complete. It also confirms to the other ten that their reluctance was the correct read of the situation.

questions.explanation: A project whose success harms the people it depends on has a purpose problem before it has a technique problem, and the standard elicitation methods all assume a participant with nothing to lose. The work is to remove the conflict rather than to design around it, which usually means forcing an organisational decision the project does not own. Where that decision cannot be brought forward, the honest position is that the knowledge is not fully obtainable and the plan should say so.
questions.mindset: When success costs a contributor their role, settle their future before asking for their knowledge.

questions.stem: A housing association completes 30,000 responsive repairs a year and currently averages 20 working days from report to completion. Your programme is funded on the case that repairs will average 14 working days, that each day of delay costs £1.40 per repair in avoidable contact and temporary accommodation, and that the new scheduling system goes live in month nine. Work the figures below and name what belongs in which category.

blanks.label: Working days saved per repair
blanks.rationale: Twenty days today against fourteen in the funded case is a saving of six working days on each repair. This is the change in the world, and it is what the funding was granted against.

blanks.label: Annual benefit in £, from the days saved
blanks.rationale: Thirty thousand repairs multiplied by six days multiplied by £1.40 gives £252,000 a year. The figure only holds if the fourteen-day average is actually reached and sustained after the programme ends.

blanks.label: Which item in the case is the programme's output rather than its benefit
blanks.rationale: The scheduling system delivered in month nine is the thing handed over, and handing it over changes nothing on its own. The benefit is the shorter wait, which arrives later and only if the way repairs are scheduled actually changes.

questions.explanation: A statement of purpose is anchored by the outcome, not the deliverable, and the two are separated by everything that has to happen after go-live. Quantifying the outcome is what makes purpose arguable rather than aspirational, but the number is a claim about behaviour after handover and needs an owner in the receiving organisation. A benefit with no named owner past go-live is a forecast nobody is obliged to make true.
questions.mindset: State the purpose as the change in the world, and name who owns it after the deliverable lands.

questions.stem: Your product exists to cut the time volunteer coordinators at a food-bank network spend building rotas. A regional manager who has championed the product since it was proposed asks for a donor-reporting dashboard. Three team members are keen because the work looks interesting, the product owner estimates about a sprint, and nothing in the backlog is urgent this week. What should you do?

options.text: Test the request against the stated purpose openly with the product owner and the requester, and if it does not serve rota time, record it as work for a different owner.
options.rationale: The purpose is applied where it costs something, in front of the person it disappoints, and the request is preserved rather than dismissed. Doing this once with a friendly stakeholder is what makes the boundary credible later with an unfriendly one.

options.text: Build it, since the capacity exists this sprint and the relationship with a long-standing champion is worth protecting.
options.rationale: It treats a quiet week as authorisation. A purpose that yields whenever there is slack does not constrain anything, and the precedent is set by the easiest case rather than the hardest.

options.text: Decline on the grounds that it falls outside the product vision, citing the vision statement in your reply.
options.rationale: The conclusion may be right and the method loses the champion. Using purpose as a door rather than a conversation forfeits the chance to find out whether the request points at a real need someone should serve.

options.text: Put it to the team to vote on, since they are the ones who would build it.
options.rationale: It resolves a question of product purpose by counting preferences among people who have already said the work looks interesting. Enthusiasm for the task is not evidence about what the product is for.

questions.explanation: A statement of purpose earns its authority the first time it is applied against something attractive, and the cases that damage it most are the popular ones rather than the obviously wrong ones. Applying it in the open, with the requester present, converts it from an internal filter into a shared standard others can use without you. Spare capacity is a fact about the calendar and never a reason about the product.
questions.mindset: A boundary is only real once it has cost you something with someone you like.

questions.stem: Your coastal flood defence exists to keep 400 homes dry in a storm surge expected roughly once a decade. The scheme may sit unused for years after handover. The design team is now arguing about an expensive instrumentation provision, and you notice the argument is being conducted entirely in terms of capital cost and programme, with no one referring to what happens in a surge. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Require the decision to be argued in terms of what each option does during a surge, using the modelled event, and bring in people from the last flood to describe it.
options.rationale: When the ultimate outcome is years away and may never be witnessed, teams substitute the goals they can see. Forcing the argument back onto the modelled event restores the only frame in which the provision can actually be judged.

options.text: Decide it on cost-benefit analysis, since the whole scheme was justified that way and the same method should settle its parts.
options.rationale: The analysis is a summary of a judgement about the surge, not a substitute for making it. Applying it to a detail nobody has framed in event terms produces a defensible number with the purpose left out of it.

options.text: Remind the team of the sponsor's public commitment to protecting the 400 homes.
options.rationale: It answers an engineering disagreement with an appeal to authority, which settles nothing technical and invites the team to treat the purpose as political cover. Commitment is not evidence about what the instrumentation does.

options.text: Accept the cost and programme framing, since those are the constraints the project is actually measured against.
options.rationale: It confuses the measures of the project with the reason for the project. Optimising to the visible constraints is exactly how a scheme is delivered on budget and fails on the day it is needed.

questions.explanation: Where the benefit lands long after the team has dispersed, purpose has no feedback loop to keep it honest, and the goals with short feedback loops quietly take its place. The countermeasure is to make the distant outcome present in the room whenever a decision touches it, through modelling, through people who have experienced the event, and through indicators visible now. Otherwise the project is steered by whatever it can measure this quarter.
questions.mindset: When the outcome is years away, deliberately bring it into the room, or the measurable will govern instead.

questions.stem: The map traces your staff induction programme from what it delivers to the objective the board holds you against. Your contract obliges the supplier to build the platform and train the administrators; finance has validated the cost-per-hire model behind the saving; the board owns the judgement about service quality. Select the link on the chain that your current plans and contracts leave with no named owner.

graphic.title: Benefits chain from induction platform to service quality objective with four connecting links
graphic.caption: Select a link. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between links, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Platform delivered to new staff being able to complete induction before their first shift
regions.rationale: This link is carried by the supply contract, which obliges the supplier to build the platform and train the administrators who run it. It is the best-covered part of the chain and the one most often mistaken for the whole of it.

regions.label: New staff able to complete induction early to fewer leavers in the first ninety days
regions.rationale: Nothing in the contract or the plan makes anyone responsible for line managers actually scheduling induction before the first shift. Capability becomes outcome only through changed behaviour, and this is where benefits chains routinely break.

regions.label: Fewer early leavers to recruitment cost saved
regions.rationale: Finance has validated the cost-per-hire model, so if early leaving falls the saving follows arithmetically. The uncertainty here is in the previous link, not this one.

regions.label: Recruitment cost saved to the board's service quality objective
regions.rationale: Attributing a saving to a strategic objective is a judgement the board explicitly owns. An unowned link is one nobody has been assigned; this one has an owner who happens to sit above you.

questions.explanation: A benefits chain is only as strong as its least-owned link, and the gap is almost always between having a capability and using it differently, because that link is behavioural and sits outside the supply contract. Delivery obligations cover the first link and financial models cover the last few, which makes the middle look sound by association. Reading a chain means asking who is accountable for each arrow, not whether each box is credible.
questions.mindset: Read a benefits chain by its arrows and ask who owns each one, not by whether the boxes look reasonable.

questions.stem: Your sponsor has told island residents, the press and your own team that the ferry scheduling programme exists to make sailings more reliable for people who depend on them. Preparing for a stage gate, you read the approved business case properly for the first time and find its benefits are almost entirely fuel and crew savings, and that the profile depends on withdrawing two lightly used sailings. Both accounts came from the same person. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Put the discrepancy to the sponsor privately, establish which account governs the programme's decisions, and get that one written where the team and the steering group can see it.
options.rationale: Two purposes cannot both govern, and until one does every trade-off will be argued from whichever account suits the arguer. Raising it privately gives the sponsor room to resolve it rather than to defend it.

options.text: Deliver to the approved business case and leave the sponsor to manage his own public messaging.
options.rationale: It treats the contradiction as somebody else's communications problem while your team plans against the version they have heard. The withdrawal of two sailings will arrive as a shock you could see coming and chose not to name.

options.text: Adopt the reliability account with the team, since it is more motivating and the savings will follow from it anyway.
options.rationale: It picks the more appealing purpose and assumes the arithmetic will cooperate. When the sailings are cut, the team learns that the version you gave them was the one you preferred rather than the one that was funded.

options.text: Raise it at the next steering group so that the inconsistency is formally on the record.
options.rationale: Escalating first puts the sponsor in front of an audience defending a discrepancy he has not yet been asked about. It converts a solvable ambiguity into a contest over credibility, and usually hardens the position you need moved.

options.text: Ask the finance lead to rework the benefit profile so it reflects the reliability purpose the sponsor has been describing.
options.rationale: It reverse-engineers the case to match the message, which misrepresents the basis on which approval was granted. The body that funded the programme is entitled to be told the purpose has changed, not shown a case retrofitted to it.

questions.explanation: When the promoted purpose and the funded purpose differ, the project has two constituencies being told different things and no stable basis for any trade-off. Resolving it is a governance act rather than a communications one: someone with authority has to say which account governs, and it has to be recorded where those planning against it can see it. The instinct to pick the more inspiring version is the failure mode, because it postpones the reckoning to the point where the difference becomes visible in what is delivered.
questions.mindset: Where two purposes are in circulation, get one named as the one that governs before planning against either.

questions.stem: Your programme's purpose, agreed with the sponsor and displayed in the contact centre, is that a rail passenger's problem is resolved at first contact. Team leaders' quarterly awards continue to be calculated on average handling time, which the operations director owns and has just reconfirmed. Advisers have started closing and reopening cases to keep the average down, and their leaders know. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Take the reopening data to the operations director and the sponsor together, and treat the measure as the thing that must change if the purpose is to stand.
options.rationale: The advisers are responding rationally to what is rewarded, so the conflict lives between two owners rather than in anyone's conduct. Bringing both owners the evidence at once is what forces a choice instead of a compromise nobody enforces.

options.text: Ask team leaders to stop the reopening practice and remind advisers what the programme is for.
options.rationale: It asks people to absorb a contradiction through willpower while the reward structure is untouched. The behaviour returns as soon as attention moves, and the purpose is discredited for having asked.

options.text: Add a first-contact resolution measure alongside handling time so both are reported.
options.rationale: Reporting two measures that pull opposite ways leaves the resolution to whichever one carries the award, which is still handling time. Adding a metric is the intervention that feels balanced and changes nothing.

options.text: Report the reopening as a data quality issue so the reported figures can be corrected.
options.rationale: It cleans the numbers and leaves the cause running. Treating a gaming signal as a reporting defect removes the evidence that would otherwise have forced the conversation about the measure.

questions.explanation: A purpose competes with whatever is measured and rewarded, and where the two disagree the reward wins without anyone deciding that it should. Gaming is therefore diagnostic rather than disciplinary: it shows precisely where the stated aim and the operative aim have come apart. The work is to reconcile them at the level where both are owned, and until that happens the displayed purpose is a description of what the organisation would like to want.
questions.mindset: Where the stated purpose and the rewarded behaviour disagree, assume the reward is the real purpose until it changes.

questions.stem: Your data platform team is fourteen people, nine of them contractors on three- to six-month engagements, and average tenure across the team is about four months. The five permanent staff can explain what the platform is for and which requests the team has previously turned down. New contractors reach competence quickly on the technology and keep proposing work the team settled against a year ago. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Make the purpose and the standing list of what the team does not build part of a first-day induction the team itself owns.
options.rationale: The exclusions are the operative half of a purpose and they are currently held only in the memory of people who were there. Putting them at the front of induction reaches every new arrival at the moment they are forming their picture.

options.text: Record the reasoning behind past scope decisions in a log that sits where a newcomer meets the work, not in a separate document.
options.rationale: Repeated proposals are a symptom of reasoning that was never written down, only lived through. A log placed in the working path lets someone find why a road is closed at the moment they start walking down it.

options.text: Make the case to the sponsor for converting contractor roles to permanent posts to reduce churn.
options.rationale: It identifies a real cause and reaches for a lever outside the project manager's gift and outside the current engagement window. Even if granted, it does nothing for the nine people already on the team.

options.text: Pair each new contractor with one of the five permanent staff for their first fortnight.
options.rationale: It routes all continuity through five people who also have delivery to do, and it keeps purpose as personal transmission rather than something the team holds. When one of the five leaves, the channel closes.

options.text: Ask the product owner to review the backlog more often so that out-of-scope proposals are filtered before they reach the team.
options.rationale: It intercepts the proposals without addressing why they are made, and it puts one person between the team and the reasoning. The team continues not to know what it is for, and merely stops saying so.

questions.explanation: Where tenure is short, purpose has to live in artefacts and induction rather than in shared memory, and the part that decays first is the record of what was decided against. Institutional knowledge that exists only in the people who were present is unavailable to the majority of a team that turns over three times a year. The fix is to place the reasoning in the path of the work rather than to defend the memory of a shrinking group.
questions.mindset: In a team that turns over fast, write down what you decided not to do and why, because that is what disappears first.

questions.stem: A museum's collection management system goes live in six weeks and the registrar's team will run it. They attended every data workshop and none of the sessions on why the system was commissioned. Reviewing their draft local procedures, you find they have reinstated a paper checking step that duplicates the system's validation, which is precisely the double-keying the project was funded to remove. They are proud of the procedures. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Work through the procedures with the registrar's team against the outcome the project was funded for, and let them redesign the steps themselves.
options.rationale: The procedures reflect a genuine picture of good practice formed without the reasoning the project was built on. Supplying the reasoning and leaving the redesign with them keeps the ownership that will decide whether the change survives go-live.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to instruct the registrar to remove the duplicate step before go-live.
options.rationale: It wins the instruction and loses the operator. A step removed under direction is reinstated informally within a month, because the people running the process still believe it is necessary.

options.text: Note the duplication as an operational decision for the receiving team, since local procedures are theirs to write.
options.rationale: It respects a boundary at the cost of the benefit the whole project exists to deliver. Autonomy over how to work is not autonomy to reinstate the problem being solved, and nobody has yet given them the information to see the difference.

options.text: Configure the system to make the paper checking step impossible so the procedure cannot be followed.
options.rationale: It uses the product to overrule people rather than convincing them, and invites a workaround outside the system where you cannot see it. It also treats an unshared purpose as a technical problem.

questions.explanation: Benefits are realised by the receiving organisation and are lost most often in the procedures it writes for itself, which are usually drafted by people included in the mechanics and excluded from the reasoning. Anyone who will operate the outcome needs the purpose as much as anyone who builds it, and needs it early enough to design their own work around it. Instruction produces compliance until attention lapses; understanding produces procedures that hold.
questions.mindset: Whoever will run it afterwards needs the reasoning, not just the training.

questions.stem: You coach two product teams and have concluded that the same intervention will not serve both. One team talks about its purpose fluently and has never turned a request down. The other has made consistent choices for a year and goes quiet when asked to explain the thread running through them. Complete each sentence with the response that fits the team described. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A team that states the product's purpose accurately and cannot name a request it would refuse most needs
A team whose decisions have been consistent with an unwritten purpose for a year, but who cannot put it into words, most needs

options.text: a walk back through recent requests to find the ones the purpose should have refused
options.rationale: This team has the words and has never applied them to anything that cost something. Real requests supply the boundary that abstract agreement never produces, and past ones can be examined without anyone defending a live proposal.

options.text: the words for what it is already doing, written down and agreed
options.rationale: Alignment held only in shared habit works until the team grows, splits or has to explain itself to a newcomer or a sponsor. Naming what is already true costs little and makes the alignment transferable.

options.text: a fresh statement of purpose agreed from scratch with its stakeholders
options.rationale: Not used. Both teams already hold a working purpose, one in words and one in practice, and starting again discards the half that works in each case. Rewriting is the reflex that treats every alignment problem as an absence.

questions.explanation: Shared purpose has two parts that fail independently: the ability to say it and the ability to decide with it. A team can hold either without the other, and the useful diagnosis is which one is missing, because the remedies point in opposite directions. Assuming absence and starting over is the response that damages a team whose alignment is real but unspoken.
questions.mindset: Establish whether a team lacks the words or lacks the boundary, because those need opposite interventions.

questions.stem: Your shared-services programme runs across sites in Sweden, Portugal and Poland, and its purpose statement was translated by a professional agency and issued in all three languages. The Polish site manager tells you the noun chosen there carries a strong connotation of cutting back, and that her staff have read the statement as an announcement about their site. The translation is accurate. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Rework the Polish wording with people from that site until it carries the intended meaning, and accept it will not be a literal rendering.
options.rationale: A purpose statement is judged by what it causes people to believe, not by its fidelity to the source text. The people who will read it are the only reliable test of what it says, and they are available.

options.text: Keep the accurate translation and add a note clarifying that no reduction at the Polish site is intended.
options.rationale: A denial attached to a statement people have already read as a threat confirms that the threat was worth denying. It also leaves the wording doing the damage on every future reading.

options.text: Issue the statement in English only across all three sites so that everyone reads the same words.
options.rationale: Identical words are not shared meaning, and this hands an advantage to whoever is most comfortable in English. Uniformity of text is being mistaken for uniformity of understanding.

options.text: Ask the agency to review the translation and provide a corrected version.
options.rationale: The agency has already produced what it was asked for and has no access to what the word does at that site. Referring a connotation problem back to a linguistic supplier repeats the mistake of treating meaning as a technical property of the text.

questions.explanation: A statement of purpose exists in the reader rather than on the page, so accuracy of language is a much weaker standard than equivalence of effect. Wherever a message crosses a language, a site or an occupational boundary, the local reading has to be tested with local people and the wording adjusted to what it does there. Insisting on a faithful common text usually produces several different meanings and one shared illusion of alignment.
questions.mindset: Test what a statement makes people believe where they are, not whether it faithfully renders what you wrote.

questions.stem: Your product exists to make it quicker for customers to book and change appointments at a chain of dental practices. In the retrospective the team notice, without much concern, that three of the last four sprints went mostly on an internal admin console used by two staff a fortnight. The work was interesting and well built, and nobody made a decision to prioritise it. What should you do?

options.text: Have the team compare the last four sprints against what the product is for, and agree how they will notice the drift sooner next time.
options.rationale: Nobody chose this, so the fix is a mechanism for noticing rather than a correction of anyone's judgement. Doing it as the team's own review keeps the standard theirs and makes the next drift visible earlier.

options.text: Move the admin console work out of the backlog and refocus the team on customer-facing items from the next sprint.
options.rationale: It corrects the symptom by instruction and leaves the mechanism that produced it untouched. The team learns that drift gets fixed for them, so the next one runs just as long.

options.text: Ask the product owner to explain how three sprints were prioritised this way.
options.rationale: It looks for a culprit for something that happened by accumulation rather than by decision. Making it one person's failure discourages the team from raising the next occurrence themselves.

options.text: Accept it, since the console is real work for real users and the sprints were fully delivered.
options.rationale: Delivery is being used as evidence of value. Everything a team builds is real work for someone, which is why the purpose exists to say which someone this product is for.

questions.explanation: Drift away from purpose is usually the sum of reasonable individual choices, none of which was ever put as a question, and it is invisible precisely because each step was defensible. The countermeasure is a periodic look back at where the effort actually went, compared against what the work is for, rather than tighter control of each decision. Effort is the honest record of priorities, and it frequently disagrees with the stated ones.
questions.mindset: Look at where the effort went, not at what was agreed, to find out what a team is actually treating as its purpose.

questions.stem: Yours is one of five projects in a programme whose single benefit is cutting ambulance handover delays at three hospitals. Your project delivers bed-state tracking. Your sponsor asks you to bring delivery forward by dropping an interface that only the patient-flow project consumes, which would leave that project unable to demonstrate its own contribution. Your project's measures would improve. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Take the trade-off to the programme, framed as its effect on handover delay rather than on either project's schedule.
options.rationale: The interface exists to serve the shared benefit, so the decision belongs at the level where that benefit is owned. Framing it in handover terms is what stops it being settled as a scheduling argument between two projects.

options.text: Drop the interface as instructed, since your sponsor has the authority to set your project's scope.
options.rationale: It treats scope authority as sufficient when the item's value sits outside the project's boundary. Every project optimising its own delivery is exactly how a programme delivers five successful projects and no benefit.

options.text: Negotiate directly with the patient-flow project manager to find a way for them to absorb the loss.
options.rationale: It keeps a programme-level decision between two project managers who each have local measures to protect. The outcome will be whatever the two can trade, which is not the same as what the benefit requires.

options.text: Keep the interface and deliver to your original date, explaining to your sponsor that the interface is not yours to remove.
options.rationale: The judgement is defensible and the method refuses a legitimate instruction without putting the question anywhere it can be decided. It leaves your sponsor with a project manager who says no rather than a decision that has been made.

questions.explanation: When several projects contribute to one benefit, each one's local success measures reward exactly the behaviour that erodes the shared outcome, and the erosion is always defensible in local terms. Anything whose value is realised outside the project boundary has to be decided outside the project boundary, and the project manager's job is to route it there in the language of the shared benefit. Doing so is neither compliance nor refusal, which are the two failures on offer.
questions.mindset: Decide a shared benefit at the level that owns it, in the language of the benefit rather than of your schedule.

questions.stem: You are reviewing the objectives section of a charter drafted by your predecessor for a school catering programme. It lists four objectives: fit out twelve kitchens, train 60 staff, publish a new menu specification, and issue revised allergen guidance. Each has a date and an owner and all four are achievable. The sponsor is happy with them. What should the project manager do before baselining?

options.text: Ask the sponsor what will be different for pupils and kitchen staff when all four are complete, and record that as the objective the four deliverables serve.
options.rationale: The four items are things the project will hand over, and none of them says what any of it is for. Establishing the intended change gives the deliverables a standard to be judged against and a basis for trading one off against another.

options.text: Baseline them, since they are specific, dated, owned and agreed with the sponsor.
options.rationale: It applies a well-formedness test to statements of the wrong kind. Deliverables can be perfectly specified and still leave the project with no way to decide anything that was not foreseen when the list was written.

options.text: Add a fifth objective capturing the intended improvement to pupil nutrition.
options.rationale: It puts the purpose alongside the deliverables as though it were another item of the same kind. The intended change is what the other four exist to produce, and listing it as a peer hides that relationship.

options.text: Convert each of the four into a measurable target with a percentage and a threshold.
options.rationale: Measuring outputs more precisely produces sharper numbers about the wrong things. A precisely quantified count of fitted kitchens still cannot tell you whether fitting the twelfth one is worth doing.

questions.explanation: Objectives written as a list of deliverables are common because deliverables are the part that is easy to agree, date and own. The cost appears the first time something has to be traded off, when a list of outputs offers no basis for choosing between them and the decision falls to whoever is most insistent. A charter needs at least one statement of the change intended in the world, and the deliverables are then arguments for how to produce it.
questions.mindset: Ask what will be different afterwards, because a list of things to hand over cannot settle a trade-off.

questions.stem: Your offshore wind construction programme works through about forty suppliers, many of whom subcontract further. The purpose agreed with the client is that the array is maintainable by small crews in poor weather, which drives dozens of detailed design choices. Your tier-one suppliers can state this. A tier-three fabricator has just delivered access hatches that meet every dimension in the drawing and cannot be opened wearing gloves. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Put the maintainability intent into the design information that travels down the chain, so it reaches whoever is making the item.
options.rationale: The fabricator complied fully with what reached them, which is the evidence that intent stopped somewhere above. Intent has to travel with the drawing, because the drawing is the only artefact that reliably reaches the person cutting metal.

options.text: Change how items like this are reviewed, so acceptance tests use a gloved hand in the conditions the crews will work in.
options.rationale: A compliant deliverable that misses the point passes any review conducted against the specification alone. Testing in the conditions the purpose describes is what makes the intent enforceable rather than aspirational.

options.text: Raise a non-conformance against the tier-three fabricator and require replacement at their cost.
options.rationale: The hatches meet the drawing, so a non-conformance is unlikely to stand and will damage a relationship over your own omission. It also treats a systemic failure of communication as one supplier's defect.

options.text: Hold a supply chain briefing day at which the programme's purpose is presented to all forty suppliers.
options.rationale: An event reaches whoever attends, which will be tier-one commercial staff rather than the people making components three tiers down. It produces a well-attended day and leaves the same gap in the same place.

options.text: Add a clause to tier-one contracts requiring them to cascade the programme's purpose to their own subcontractors.
options.rationale: It creates an obligation without a mechanism and makes compliance unverifiable. Purpose passed on as a contractual duty tends to arrive as a paragraph nobody reads rather than as information that changes a design choice.

questions.explanation: In a tiered supply chain the people whose hands are on the work are furthest from where the purpose was agreed, and each tier passes on the specification because the specification is what it is contractually obliged to pass on. Intent therefore has to be carried by the artefacts that travel and enforced by acceptance conducted in the conditions the purpose describes. Briefings and cascade clauses address the tier you can see rather than the tier that made the thing.
questions.mindset: Send purpose down a supply chain in the artefacts that travel, and check for it in how you accept the work.

questions.stem: You have run the same product for eight months and believe the team is well aligned: the purpose is discussed often, nobody disputes it, and planning is easy. A colleague asks how you know the alignment is real rather than polite. You cannot immediately answer, and you notice that the team has never disagreed with each other about a prioritisation decision in front of you. What is the best way to test it?

options.text: Put a genuinely contested request to individuals separately, ask each what the purpose implies, and compare the answers.
options.rationale: Alignment is only observable where it has to discriminate, so the test needs a hard case rather than a restatement. Asking separately removes the convergence that a room produces regardless of what people privately think.

options.text: Run an anonymous survey asking how clearly the team understands the product's purpose.
options.rationale: It collects confidence rather than content, and people who have understood the same words differently will all report understanding them clearly. The measure cannot detect the failure it is meant to find.

options.text: Ask the team in the next retrospective whether everyone feels aligned on the purpose.
options.rationale: It asks the question in the setting most likely to produce agreement, in front of the person who set the direction. The absence of open disagreement is the thing already in doubt, so the retrospective cannot be the instrument.

options.text: Accept the evidence you have, since frictionless planning over eight months is a strong signal in itself.
options.rationale: Easy planning is equally consistent with real alignment and with deference, and the two look identical from the front of the room. Treating the absence of conflict as proof of agreement is the assumption being questioned.

questions.explanation: Agreement observed in groups is unreliable because groups converge for reasons that have nothing to do with shared understanding, and confidence measures cannot distinguish a shared reading from several confident private ones. Testing alignment requires a case where the purpose must exclude something and answers gathered where people are not adjusting to each other. Long stretches without disagreement are weak evidence of alignment and reasonable evidence that disagreement is not being voiced.
questions.mindset: Test alignment on a hard case answered privately, because harmony in a room is not evidence of a shared view.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the line of sight from your workstreams up to the corporate objective. Two of your workstreams disagree about whether a shared patient record should be optimised for speed of first contact or completeness of clinical history. Speed serves your own programme's outcome; completeness serves a second programme's outcome, and that programme also consumes the record. Select the level at which this disagreement must be resolved.

graphic.title: Four-level line of sight from workstreams through project and programmes to a corporate objective
graphic.caption: Select a level. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between levels, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Workstream level — four delivery workstreams
regions.rationale: The two workstreams can describe the trade-off precisely and neither has any standing to rule on which outcome matters more. Leaving it here produces a technical argument that stands in for a decision nobody is authorised to make.

regions.label: Project level — the shared patient record project
regions.rationale: It is your project, which makes this the intuitive answer, but the competing claim comes from outside the project boundary. Deciding here settles a claim belonging to someone who is not in the room.

regions.label: Programme level — your programme, one of three
regions.rationale: Your programme owns only one of the two outcomes in contention, so a decision at this level resolves the question in its own favour by construction. Authority over one side of a trade-off is not authority over the trade-off.

regions.label: Corporate objective — the level holding all three programmes
regions.rationale: This is the lowest level at which both contested outcomes are owned by the same body, which is what a decision between them requires. Anything lower can only assert a preference on behalf of one side.

questions.explanation: A disagreement about design is often a disagreement about which outcome the work is for, and it can only be settled where every outcome in contention has the same owner. The rule is to find the lowest common parent of the competing claims rather than the level nearest the argument, and the frequent error is deciding at the level that happens to be yours. Where two purposes meet below their shared owner, whoever decides is choosing which purpose counts.
questions.mindset: Take a clash of purposes to the lowest level that owns both of them, not to the level that owns you.

questions.stem: A heritage railway trust's programme exists to raise year-round visitor capacity so the line stops depending on six summer weekends. A donor offering a fifth of the remaining funding wants their money spent restoring a particular locomotive, which would run on those same summer weekends. Two trustees are enthusiastic. The programme has no other route to the shortfall. What should the project manager advise?

options.text: Set out for the trustees what the donation does and does not do for year-round capacity, so they decide knowingly whether to change the purpose or decline the terms.
options.rationale: The choice belongs to the trustees and is currently being made without the conflict being named. Putting the incompatibility in front of them converts a drift into a decision that someone is accountable for.

options.text: Accept the donation and treat the locomotive as an additional benefit alongside the capacity objective.
options.rationale: It admits work that serves a different purpose by relabelling it as a bonus. A fifth of the funding attached to summer weekends will pull scope, attention and future donor expectation towards the thing the programme was set up to stop depending on.

options.text: Decline the donation on the grounds that it does not serve the agreed purpose.
options.rationale: The judgement may well be right and it is not the project manager's to make. Refusing a fifth of the funding on your own authority takes a trustee-level decision about the organisation's direction.

options.text: Accept the donation and negotiate with the donor afterwards to redirect part of it towards capacity work.
options.rationale: It banks the money on terms you intend to renegotiate later from a weaker position. The donor has been specific, and treating that as an opening offer risks both the funding and the trust's reputation with other donors.

questions.explanation: Funding with conditions attached is a proposal to change the purpose, whatever it is called, and the damage is done by leaving that unstated rather than by the change itself. The project manager's job is to make the incompatibility legible to the people with authority over the purpose, in terms of what the money buys against what the programme exists for. Both accepting quietly and refusing unilaterally take that decision away from them.
questions.mindset: Money with strings is a proposal to change the purpose; name it as one and let the owners decide.

questions.stem: A county record office is digitising its archive. The grant that funds the work emphasises public engagement, and the archivists who do the work understand the purpose as long-term preservation. Both readings are defensible and the team has been quietly resolving the tension item by item, choosing preservation-grade capture for material nobody has requested in twenty years. The grant's first review is in two months. What should you do?

options.text: Get the two purposes stated together and ranked for the cases where they conflict, with the funder and the archive's leadership in the same conversation.
options.rationale: Two legitimate purposes need an order of precedence, not a winner, and only the people who hold them can set it. Doing it before the review means the ranking is agreed rather than imposed by a disappointing report.

options.text: Reprioritise the backlog towards frequently requested material so the review shows engagement outcomes.
options.rationale: It resolves a genuine conflict of purpose by predicting what an audit will reward. The archivists' reading is not thereby answered, and the team will read the change as the funder's view winning without discussion.

options.text: Keep the current approach and explain the preservation rationale at the review.
options.rationale: It defends a choice the team has been making without a mandate, in front of the body whose money rests on a different reading. The moment to establish the priority was before spending two months of effort on it.

options.text: Split the team so one group works to engagement and the other to preservation.
options.rationale: It gives each purpose a constituency and removes any need to reconcile them. Structural separation converts a conflict that could be settled once into a permanent negotiation over capacity.

questions.explanation: Where two defensible purposes coexist, the failure is rarely that the wrong one wins; it is that neither is stated so the choice is made repeatedly, invisibly, by whoever is doing the work. A shared purpose in these cases is a stated precedence covering the cases where the two collide, agreed by the parties who hold each. Anything else leaves a team resolving a governance question one item at a time.
questions.mindset: When two purposes are both legitimate, agree which yields when they collide, rather than choosing between them.

questions.stem: Your sponsor tells you in confidence that the fleet systems project you are running is preparation for a possible sale of the division, which is why the data must be clean and the interfaces documented to an unusual standard. She instructs you not to share this. Your team keep asking why the documentation bar is so high for a system with two years of life left, and you have been answering vaguely. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Go back to the sponsor with what the team is asking and what your vagueness is costing, and agree what can honestly be said about the standard without disclosing the sale.
options.rationale: Confidentiality binds the specific fact, not every explanation, and a truthful narrower reason usually exists. Renegotiating the boundary is the only route that neither breaks the confidence nor leaves you improvising.

options.text: Tell the team the standard is a corporate requirement you are not able to explain further.
options.rationale: It is honest and it abandons the attempt to give the work meaning, which is the thing actually in your gift. Teams told to comply without reasons meet the letter of a documentation standard and little more.

options.text: Tell the team in confidence, since they will work better knowing and they can be trusted.
options.rationale: It substitutes your judgement for the sponsor's on a disclosure that is not yours to make, and puts the team under a confidence they did not accept. Trust in the team is not the question; authority over the information is.

options.text: Continue giving vague answers and rely on the documentation standard being met because it is mandated.
options.rationale: Vagueness from a project manager who plainly knows more is read accurately, and what it teaches is that questions here get managed. The cost is not one unanswered question but the credibility of every future explanation.

questions.explanation: A purpose that cannot be fully disclosed is a common situation and it does not license either leaking or stonewalling. The workable position is a true statement at a level you are permitted to give, negotiated with whoever owns the confidence, plus honesty about the existence of a boundary rather than a pretence that there is nothing behind it. Evasion costs more than the withheld fact, because it teaches people to discount everything else you say.
questions.mindset: When you cannot give the whole reason, negotiate a true partial one rather than improvising an evasion.

questions.stem: A council's planning service handled 200 validation cases last quarter: 180 were completed in 10 working days and 20 took 60 working days. The programme's stated purpose is to stop applicants being left waiting months, and the objective as written commits to reducing the average validation time. Work the figures and decide which measure matches the stated intent.

blanks.label: Mean validation time in working days
blanks.rationale: One hundred and eighty cases at ten days plus twenty at sixty days is 3,000 days across 200 cases, giving a mean of 15. No individual applicant experienced anything close to this figure.

blanks.label: Percentage of cases already completed within 10 working days
blanks.rationale: One hundred and eighty of 200 is 90%. The service is already fast for nine cases in ten, which is why an average is a poor description of the problem the programme exists to solve.

blanks.label: Which measure matches the stated intent — the mean, or the number of cases beyond 10 days
accept: the number of cases beyond 10 days
the number of cases over 10 days
blanks.rationale: The purpose names people left waiting months, which is the 20 slow cases. The mean can be improved by making fast cases marginally faster, leaving every applicant the programme cares about exactly where they were.

questions.explanation: A measure is a claim about which change counts, so a measure that can be satisfied without helping the people named in the purpose is not a weak measure but a different objective wearing the same words. Distributions with a long tail break averages in exactly this way, and the tail is usually where the stated intent lives. Checking that the measure cannot be met in a way that leaves the purpose unserved is part of agreeing the purpose, not a refinement afterwards.
questions.mindset: Ask how a target could be hit while the purpose goes unserved, and treat any such route as a fault in the measure.

questions.stem: You run a prison education programme. The commissioning contract defines success as attendance hours, which is what the funding is paid against and what the ministry reports publicly. Your tutors say the point is that people leave with work, and have begun steering learners towards a construction certificate with lower attendance and far better employment outcomes. Attendance is falling, funding is at risk, and the tutors are right. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Gather the employment evidence the tutors are generating and take it to the commissioner as a case for changing what the contract measures, while being explicit that attendance is falling now.
options.rationale: The tutors have produced the one thing that can move a contractual measure, which is evidence that the proxy is failing its own intent. Disclosing the fall is what makes it a case rather than a defence discovered later.

options.text: Instruct tutors to restore attendance to contract levels while the employment approach is discussed separately.
options.rationale: It protects the funding by requiring people to do work they can demonstrate is worse for learners. Compliance bought this way is not recoverable later, because the tutors will have learned what the programme actually rewards.

options.text: Let the tutors continue and report attendance without drawing attention to the shortfall until the outcome data is stronger.
options.rationale: It relies on the commissioner not noticing a contracted measure, which converts a defensible professional judgement into a concealment. When the shortfall surfaces, the employment evidence will be read as an excuse constructed afterwards.

options.text: Ask the tutors to run both approaches so attendance holds and employment outcomes accumulate as evidence.
options.rationale: It defers the conflict by spending capacity that does not exist and leaves the contradiction operating on every learner decision. Doing both is the answer that avoids naming which purpose governs.

options.text: Escalate to your own sponsor to secure cover for the funding risk before approaching the commissioner.
options.rationale: It arranges internal protection while the commissioner, who owns the measure, continues to be paid against something the programme has stopped delivering. Sequencing it this way makes the eventual disclosure look managed.

questions.explanation: Contracted proxies are agreed because the real outcome is hard to measure in year, and they become the purpose by default the moment money attaches to them. When front-line practice diverges from the proxy in favour of the underlying intent, the situation is a case for renegotiation supported by evidence, made openly and early, with the cost of the divergence stated. Suppressing either the practice or the shortfall converts a defensible position into an indefensible one.
questions.mindset: When a measure and the purpose it stands for come apart, argue it openly with evidence rather than quietly choosing one.

questions.stem: Your team has just shipped the third release of an ordering platform for a brewery's trade customers, whose purpose is to let a publican reorder in under a minute from a phone behind the bar. You are writing the short note that goes to the team, the sponsor and the four pilot publicans. The release delivered saved baskets, a redesigned login and two performance fixes. What is the best way to frame it?

options.text: Lead with what a publican can now do that they could not last month, then list the changes that made it possible.
options.rationale: It reports the release in the terms the product exists in, and does so at the moment people are paying attention. The features remain visible, but as means rather than as the achievement.

options.text: List the three changes with a short technical note on each, since the audience includes the team who built them.
options.rationale: It reports effort to people who need to know what the effort bought. Teams that only ever see their work described as a list of components gradually come to measure themselves that way.

options.text: Report the reorder time achieved in pilot against the under-a-minute target, and leave the changes out.
options.rationale: The number is the right subject and stripping the work loses the connection the note exists to make. The team cannot see their contribution in it, and the publicans cannot see what changed.

options.text: Thank the team for a strong sprint and confirm the next release date.
options.rationale: Recognition without content leaves everyone with the impression that delivery itself is the achievement. It uses one of the few moments of guaranteed attention on something that teaches nothing about the purpose.

questions.explanation: Milestones are the cheapest reinforcement available because the audience is already assembled and interested, and they are routinely spent on lists of what was built. Framing each one as the change now possible keeps purpose attached to real evidence rather than to restatement, and gives the team a way of describing their work that is not a component inventory. What gets narrated at milestones becomes what people believe the work is for.
questions.mindset: Describe what a milestone made possible, not what it contained.

questions.stem: The project management office has drafted the agenda for your two-day kickoff for a laboratory relocation. It allocates 90 minutes to scope, 90 to schedule, 60 to risks and issues, and 30 to introductions, and the remaining time to breakout planning by workstream. Everything on it is useful. The forty attendees include people from three departments who have not worked together before. Which two changes should the project manager make?

options.text: Open with the sponsor setting out what the relocation is for and taking questions on it, before any planning session runs.
options.rationale: Planning sessions are where the purpose is spent, so it has to be established first and by the person who owns it. Putting it after scope means each breakout starts from its own assumption about the point of the work.

options.text: Replace part of the breakout time with a session where the three departments state what a good outcome looks like from where they sit.
options.rationale: Three groups who have not worked together will hold different pictures of success, and the differences are cheapest to find on day one. It also gives each group a stake in a purpose they helped phrase.

options.text: Extend the introductions so that all forty attendees can introduce themselves properly.
options.rationale: It improves the social opening without touching what people believe the project is for. Familiarity between individuals is not the same as a shared picture of the work.

options.text: Add a session on the governance structure and the escalation route so everyone knows how decisions will be made.
options.rationale: Useful information that answers how decisions travel rather than what they should serve. It is the addition that feels responsible and leaves the day still without a stated purpose.

options.text: Circulate the charter in advance so the purpose is understood before anyone arrives.
options.rationale: Pre-reading reaches those who read it and produces no shared moment or opportunity to disagree. It also uses the kickoff's scarcest asset, everyone in one room, on everything except the thing hardest to align remotely.

questions.explanation: A kickoff is the one occasion when everyone who will make decisions on a project is present at once, and its agenda records what the organisation thinks is hard. Scope, schedule and risk can all be worked afterwards in smaller groups; a shared picture of the point of the work, and the disagreement about it, cannot. Whatever the kickoff does first is also what participants infer the project is really about.
questions.mindset: Spend the one hour everyone is in the room on the thing that cannot be aligned any other way.

questions.stem: Your battery storage project was justified on two benefits: arbitrage revenue, which carried the case, and grid stability services, which was listed as secondary. A grid code change published last month has roughly tripled the value of the stability services and left arbitrage broadly flat. Nobody has raised it. Your design decisions over the next two months lock in which of the two the plant is optimised for. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Put the revised benefit picture to the sponsor and steering group now, with the design decisions that depend on it and the date they close.
options.rationale: The purpose has changed in the world and not in the project, and the window for acting on it is defined by the design lock. Presenting the deadline alongside the change is what turns an interesting fact into a decision.

options.text: Continue to the approved business case, since it is the basis on which funding was granted and nothing has been formally changed.
options.rationale: It treats the case as a specification to be complied with rather than a claim about value that can go out of date. Delivering faithfully to a case everyone knows is stale is a way of being blameless rather than useful.

options.text: Optimise the design for stability services, since the evidence clearly supports it, and update the business case afterwards.
options.rationale: It changes what the project is for on the project manager's own authority. The evidence may be strong, but reweighting the benefits is a decision for whoever approved them, and doing it first makes the update a formality.

options.text: Raise it at the benefits review scheduled after the design phase, when the impact can be quantified properly.
options.rationale: It observes the governance calendar past the point at which the decision is still available. A review held after the design locks can only record which option was foreclosed.

questions.explanation: A purpose agreed at approval has a shelf life, and the events that change its value usually happen outside the project and get noticed by nobody whose job it is to act. Keeping purpose current means watching for those changes and, more importantly, knowing when the decisions they bear on close, because the value of raising it collapses at that point. The two failure modes are delivering faithfully to a superseded case and quietly substituting your own.
questions.mindset: Raise a change in what the work is worth while the decisions it affects are still open.

questions.stem: During refinement a developer asks why the team is building an address-lookup feature for a veterinary practice booking product, given how small the time saving looks.
