You know the answer: mistyped addresses are the main reason home-visit vets arrive at the wrong property, which costs an hour each time. How should you answer?

options.text: Explain what mistyped addresses currently cost a visiting vet, and let the team judge the story against that.
options.rationale: It supplies the outcome the story serves and hands the judgement back to the people who will build it. The developer asked a good question and gets information rather than reassurance.

options.text: Explain that the practice managers asked for it and it is high on the backlog.
options.rationale: It answers with the origin of the request rather than its value, which teaches the team that provenance settles priority. The same question then recurs on every story a stakeholder has named.

options.text: Suggest the developer raise it with the product owner, who owns prioritisation.
options.rationale: It routes a question you can answer into someone else's queue and signals that reasons are dispensed by role. Refinement is exactly where a story's purpose is supposed to be examined.

options.text: Note the concern and propose the team try the feature and measure the saving after release.
options.rationale: It defers a question that has an answer available now, and spends a sprint finding out something already known. Measuring afterwards is right when nobody knows, which is not the case here.

questions.explanation: Most reinforcement of purpose happens in unremarkable moments rather than in set-piece communications, and a question in refinement is the cheapest of them. Answering with the outcome, rather than with who asked or how it ranks, is what gradually gives a team the ability to make these judgements without the project manager present. Answering with provenance trains the opposite habit.
questions.mindset: Answer why with the outcome it serves, not with who asked for it.

questions.stem: You are explaining the same product's purpose to three audiences this week, and your instinct is to give all three the version you use with the steering group. A colleague points out that each of them will need it for a different job afterwards. Match each audience to the framing that will do most work with them. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A dispatcher whose daily routine the product will visibly change.
The finance director who has to defend the continued investment.
A developer joining the team next week.

options.text: What a shift will look like once this works, and which parts of the current job disappear.
options.rationale: Someone whose routine is changing needs the purpose in the concrete terms of their own day, including the losses. Abstract benefit language reads as evasion to the person who can already see what will change.

options.text: The outcome being bought, what it is worth, and how it will be evidenced.
options.rationale: A finance director must restate the purpose to people who were not there, so they need the version that survives a challenge. Quantified value and its evidence are what makes that restatement possible.

options.text: The decisions the purpose has already settled, and the requests it has ruled out.
options.rationale: A newcomer needs the operative boundary rather than the sentence, because that is what governs the work they are about to pick up. Past exclusions convey it faster than any statement of intent.

options.text: The delivery milestones and the date the product goes live.
options.rationale: Not used. Schedule answers when rather than what for, and it is the substitution that gets made with every audience because it is always available. None of the three needs it to understand the purpose.

questions.explanation: One statement of purpose does not serve every audience, because each needs it for a different job: to anticipate a change to their work, to defend it to others, or to make decisions with it. The content is the same and the framing follows the use, so the question to ask before speaking is what this person will have to do with what they are told. Substituting the schedule is the default when that question is not asked.
questions.mindset: Frame purpose around what the listener will have to do with it.

questions.stem: Your hospital pharmacy system has gone live at three of eleven sites. At two in the morning a fault delays dispensing at one site by around forty minutes per order; the workaround is safe but slow. On the incident call the supplier argues for holding the rollout to protect the contracted schedule, and your programme office argues for rolling back all three sites to protect the launch record. The programme exists to eliminate dispensing errors. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reframe the decision around whether patients are safer with the fault, the workaround or a rollback, and require both arguments to be made in those terms.
options.rationale: Both positions are optimising for things the programme was never for, and neither party will change frame unaided at two in the morning. Restating the criterion is the contribution available to the project manager here and it changes what counts as a good argument.

options.text: Roll back the three sites, since reverting to a known state is the safest action under uncertainty.
options.rationale: It adopts a general heuristic without asking whether the known state is safer here, when the old process is the one that produced the error rate the programme exists to remove. Reverting is a decision about risk and needs the same test as any other.

options.text: Hold the rollout at three sites and continue with the workaround while the fault is diagnosed.
options.rationale: It may well be the right outcome and it is being reached by picking the supplier's position rather than by applying a criterion. Choosing between two badly framed arguments leaves the next decision equally unanchored.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor for a decision, given the clinical risk and the disagreement on the call.
options.rationale: It moves an unframed question upwards, so the sponsor receives the same schedule-versus-record argument with more authority attached. Escalation adds value once the decision has a criterion, not instead of one.

questions.explanation: Under time pressure people argue from what they are individually accountable for, and a shared purpose is precisely what stops that producing an incoherent decision. The project manager's contribution is often not the answer but the criterion, stated in time to shape which arguments are admissible. A purpose that is not used in the hardest hour of the project has not been established, whatever was agreed when things were calm.
questions.mindset: In a crisis, supply the criterion rather than the answer, because everyone else is arguing from their own accountability.

questions.stem: You review the charters of two projects approved in the same portfolio this quarter. Neither is badly run and both sponsors are engaged, yet in each case something in the statement of purpose stops it from guiding a decision, and the two gaps are not the same. Complete each sentence with what is missing in the situation described. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A new stakeholder asks what the project will change and the only answer available is the list of deliverables. What is missing is
The intended change is clearly stated and nobody can say whose life it is meant to improve. What is missing is

options.text: a statement of what will be different once the deliverables are in use
options.rationale: A list of outputs describes what will be handed over and says nothing about the change it is meant to produce. Supplying that statement is what gives the deliverables something to be judged against.

options.text: the named group the change is for, agreed with someone who represents them
options.rationale: An improvement with no beneficiary can be claimed by anyone and verified by no one. Naming the group makes it possible to ask them whether the change has actually happened.

options.text: a more detailed breakdown of the deliverables and their dependencies
options.rationale: Not used. More precision about outputs answers neither question, and it is the usual response to both because it is the work a project team is already equipped to do.

questions.explanation: A usable purpose answers two questions that fail independently: which change the work is meant to produce, and which group is supposed to notice it. Either can be absent while the other reads convincingly, so a statement that survives one test is not thereby sound. Elaborating the outputs is the reflex response to both gaps, because it is the work a project team is already equipped to do and it always feels like progress.
questions.mindset: A purpose needs both a change and someone it changes things for; check for each separately.

questions.stem: A product is funded jointly by two organisations, each with an executive sponsor on the steering group. One consistently describes the product as a way to win customers from a competitor; the other consistently describes it as a way to cut the cost of serving existing ones. Both are content, both are right about their own organisation's reason for investing, and your team is now making design choices that serve one at the expense of the other. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Bring both sponsors to the same conversation with two or three real decisions where the readings diverge, rather than raising it in the abstract.
options.rationale: Stated in general terms both purposes sound compatible and neither sponsor has any reason to concede. Concrete decisions are what make the incompatibility undeniable and force it to be settled rather than acknowledged.

options.text: Get a written precedence covering the cases where the two conflict, and a named route for decisions that the precedence does not cover.
options.rationale: The team needs something it can apply without convening two executives, and no rule will anticipate every case. Precedence plus a route handles both the foreseeable conflicts and the ones that are not.

options.text: Follow the sponsor whose organisation contributes the larger share of the funding.
options.rationale: It settles a question of purpose by weight of money without either party agreeing that this is how it will be settled. The smaller partner discovers the rule only when a decision goes against them.

options.text: Work with each sponsor separately so that neither is put in the position of conceding in front of the other.
options.rationale: Separate conversations are what allowed two purposes to coexist unchallenged, and continuing them keeps the conflict inside the delivery team. Protecting executives from a disagreement they own transfers it to people with no authority to resolve it.

options.text: Ask the team to weigh both purposes in each design decision and document how they balanced them.
options.rationale: It delegates an unresolved governance question to the people least able to answer it, and the documentation records the problem rather than solving it. Balancing is not available when the two point in opposite directions on a specific choice.

questions.explanation: Two sponsors with different reasons for funding the same work is a stable arrangement until a decision separates them, which is why it usually surfaces first as design churn rather than as an argument. Resolution needs both parties present, concrete cases to make the conflict real, and an outcome recorded as a precedence the team can apply alone. Asking the team to hold both purposes in balance sounds even-handed and simply relocates the failure.
questions.mindset: Two purposes look compatible until a real decision separates them; use the decision to force the choice.

questions.stem: Your team is rolling out a new stock app to nine stores in waves. The launch briefing explaining what the app is for has been run at three stores, covering 210 of the chain's 640 shop-floor staff. The programme report currently states that the launch has been communicated. Work the coverage figures and decide what the report should say.

blanks.label: Percentage of shop-floor staff who have received the briefing, to one decimal place
blanks.rationale: Two hundred and ten of 640 is 32.8%. Three stores out of nine sounds like a third of the job done, and by people it is roughly the same, which is a coincidence rather than a reason to report stores.

blanks.label: Number of shop-floor staff not yet briefed
blanks.rationale: Six hundred and forty less 210 leaves 430 people who will meet the app without having heard what it is for. That number, not the count of sessions delivered, is the size of the remaining problem.

blanks.label: Which figure the report should carry — the number of briefings delivered, or the proportion of staff reached
blanks.rationale: Counting sessions measures the project's activity, while counting people measures whether anyone was reached. A report that says communication has happened, on the evidence of three sessions, is describing effort as though it were effect.

questions.explanation: Communication is routinely reported as activity delivered because activity is what the project controls and can count. The meaningful figure is the share of the affected population that has actually received the message, and it is usually far lower than the sense of progress inside the team. Stating coverage as a proportion of people also identifies who remains, which is the only version of the number that tells anyone what to do next.
questions.mindset: Report communication as the share of people reached, not as the number of sessions run.

questions.stem: Three programme managers have asked you to review their statements of purpose ahead of a portfolio assurance review. Each statement has been approved, is quoted regularly and is admired by the people who wrote it, and none of the three has ever settled an argument. Match each statement to the defect that prevents it from guiding a decision. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: To become the region's most trusted provider of home care.
To deliver the new rostering system to all forty branches by March.
To improve efficiency, quality and staff satisfaction while reducing cost.

options.text: It states an ambition for the organisation and settles nothing inside the programme.
options.rationale: Every option a programme could take is consistent with becoming more trusted, so the statement excludes nothing. Statements pitched at the organisation's identity are agreed easily for exactly that reason.

options.text: It names what will be handed over and when, and never says what will be different.
options.rationale: A deliverable and a date can be fully achieved while nothing improves for anyone. This defect is the hardest to see because the statement is specific, dated and easy to track.

options.text: It names several aims that will conflict and gives no order between them.
options.rationale: Efficiency, quality, satisfaction and cost pull against each other in most real decisions, and without a precedence each decision is settled by whoever is in the room. Listing aims together is often a way of avoiding the ranking.

options.text: It names a beneficiary group so wide that nobody could be excluded from it.
options.rationale: Not used. None of the three names a beneficiary at all, and naming one too broadly is a different fault from omitting one. It is worth distinguishing, because the remedy is narrowing rather than adding.

questions.explanation: Statements of purpose fail in a small number of recognisable ways: pitched too high to exclude anything, written as outputs so nothing is said about change, or listing aims that conflict without ranking them. Each has a different remedy, which is why naming the defect matters more than judging the statement good or bad. A statement can be admired by everyone who reads it and still be incapable of settling a single argument.
questions.mindset: When a statement of purpose is not working, name which way it fails before trying to rewrite it.

questions.stem: Your tram extension was approved to reduce city-centre congestion. Through consultation, residents' groups along the route have consistently argued that the real value is access to the hospital from a ward with poor transport, and support for the scheme is plainly strongest on those grounds. The design would need modest changes to serve it well. Your sponsor has not been asked about any of this. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Establish what the access outcome would require of the design and what it would cost, then put it to the sponsor as a decision about the scheme's purpose.
options.rationale: Consultation has produced evidence about value that the approving body has never seen, and it is only actionable with the design implications attached. Framing it as a purpose decision puts it where it can be authorised.

options.text: Tell the residents' groups plainly what has and has not been decided, and by whom, so the consultation is not read as agreement.
options.rationale: Groups whose framing has been listened to sympathetically will reasonably assume it has been accepted. Being explicit about the state of the decision protects both their trust and the sponsor's freedom to say no.

options.text: Adopt the hospital access framing in the scheme's public communications, since it is where the support is.
options.rationale: It changes what the scheme is for on the strength of popularity and without any authority to do so. It also commits the project publicly to an outcome the design does not yet deliver.

options.text: Record the access argument as consultation feedback and continue delivering the approved congestion purpose.
options.rationale: It files evidence that the approved purpose may be the less valuable one and treats consultation as a procedural step to be completed. The information reaches an archive rather than the person who could act on it.

options.text: Commission further consultation to establish how widely the access framing is held before raising it.
options.rationale: It buys certainty about something already consistent across groups, at the cost of the design window. More evidence is the reasonable-sounding way of postponing a decision somebody has to make.

questions.explanation: Consultation regularly discovers that the value the affected population sees is not the one the scheme was approved for, and that discovery is a governance input rather than a mandate. The project manager's task is to convert it into a decision the sponsor can take, complete with design and cost implications, while being candid with the people consulted about what has not yet been agreed. Adopting the new framing directly and filing it away are opposite failures with the same cause.
questions.mindset: Treat a better purpose found in consultation as a decision to be put to whoever owns it, not as a mandate or as feedback to file.
